newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: MACFARLANE SAYS PM A LONG WAY FROM CONVINCING FARMERS
Queensland Graingrowers President, Ian MacFarlane, says farmers won't change their line that pastoral leases must extinguish native title.

Mr MacFarlane says the Prime Minister is a long way from convincing farmers, and refused to reveal the details of his 10-point plan when he addressed about two-thousand farmers at Longreach on the weekend.
Mr MacFarlane told ABC Radio, farmers are willing to negotiate on some aspects of the plan, but their bottom line on extinguishment won't change.
REITH SAYS NO PLAN FOR DOUBLE DISSOLUTION

Industrial Relations minister Peter Reith says the Government doesn't have a plan for a double dissolution, although he says one could be triggered if the Senate refuses to pass the unfair dismissal changes.
The Government wants to exempt small businesses from compliance with unfair dismissal laws.
Mr Reith says the Government is simply facing up to political reality.
He says if the Senate gives the Government a hard time with the measures it puts forward, then the Government's entitled to stockpile them as double dissolution triggers.
On native title, Mr Reith says John Howard has put forward a fair deal for both pastoralists and claimants.
ICAC TO INVESTIGATE JAIL BREAK ATTEMPT AT MAITLAND
The weekend jail break attempt, by drug trafficer, George Savvas, and serial killer Ivan Millat will be investigated by New South Wales' Independent Commission Against Corruption.
A Commission spokesman says investigators are intent on discovering whether there was any involvement by prison officers.
The prisoners, and two other violent inmates a Maitland prison were planning the escape, and after if was foiled, George Savass was found hanged in his cell.
Police have launched their own investigation into the matter, and a coronial inquest and a departmental inquiry are also underway into the death of Savvas.
NATIONAL TRUNK RAILWAY TO BE DISCUSSED AT MINISTERS' MEET

The Transport Ministers' Council on Thursday is expected to consider a proposal for a feasibility study for a national trunk railway through inland Victoria, New South Wales, Queensland and the Northern Territory.
The executive of a group of councils pushing the scheme, Barry Donaldson, says private enterprise is ready to look at the project if it's proved feasible.
The council meets in Cairns on Thursday.
REITH SAYS UNION OPPOSITION TO A GST UNDERSTANDABLE
The Federal Industrial Relations Minister says opposition to a Goods and Services Tax from the union movement is understandable.
Peter Reith says a G-S-T would ensure that many of those in unions who are paid in cash, could no longer avoid paying tax.
Mr Reith says the last thing people operating in the cash economy want to do is pay their fair share of taxes.
He says he expects those people will use their political muscle in the labour movement to ensure the Labor Party creates a juicy scare campaign against a GST.
FOUNDATION CRITICISES MOVE TO EXPEL DRUG-TAKING STUDENTS
The Australian Drug Foundation says moves to expel students from a Victorian school after they were found to be using herion, won't do anything to help the students.
A surveillance camera hidden near a wash basin at the Glen Eira secondary college recorded the boys injecting heroin.

Foundation chief, Geoff Munro says expelling those students, who he says were probably just experimenting, would label them for life, and end their education career prematurely. Mr Munro says the move won't reduce drug use in schools, and would increase the possibility of sustained drug use later in life.
He says while schools can't condone such behaviour, they need to take into account the effects of their action on the futures of those involved.
Meanwhile, police say there's a prima facie case against the boys, and are likely to lay charges over the incident.
PRISON OFFICERS ASSOCIATION SAYS OFFICERS WERE AT RISK
The Prison Officers Association says Maitland Jail management put officers at risk by not acting earlier to stop an escape bid by Ivan Milat and George Savvas.
Corrective Services operations chief Ron Woodham says the ICAC, police and prison authorities had been monitoring Savvas and Milat for several weeks after learning of the escape plot.
The actual escape was thwarted on Saturday, and yesterday Savvas was found hanging in his cell.

Prison Officers Association Official John Doyle told ABC Radio, authorities seemed to know in advance that the pair planned to overpower prison officers during the escape, and that Ivan Milat was desperate enough to kill.
COMMITTEE SET UP TO CRACK DOWN ON SOCCER VIOLENCE
A special committee's been established in an effort to crackdown on violence at soccer matches.
Brawls erupted during yesterday's Ericsson Cup preliminary final between Sydney United and South Melbourne at Paramatta Stadium.
Five police were injured and three-men arrested and charged over the violence.
Police say a review committee's been set up involving representatives from police, soccer officials and Paramatta Stadium.
It'll examine measures to ensure there's not a repeat of yesterday's violence.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
